description: How four COVID vaccine makers turned zero into tens of billions — then watched the money dry up. Annual vaccine revenue (Comirnaty / Spikevax / Vaxzevria / Janssen) 2005–2024, in billions USD.
youtube_description:
The Vaccine Jackpot — visualized (2005–2024)

00:00 Intro — Why vaccines became a $100B race
00:28 The decade of zero — 2005–2019 (no COVID vaccine revenue)
01:05 2020 — first emergency approvals, down payments & advance buys
02:00 2021 — the jackpot: Pfizer $36.8B, Moderna $18.4B, AstraZeneca $3.7B, J&J $0.5B
03:10 2022 — grim math: big drop but still huge (Pfizer ~$32B; Moderna ~$8B)
04:05 2023 — boosters slump: Pfizer $14.6B; Moderna $3.4B; AZ & J&J near zero
05:00 2024 — what’s left: updated shots, smaller markets, new pricing
05:40 Conclusions — who won, who was crushed, what this means for future pandemic pharma
06:20 Sources & notes

Key story: From near-zero to tens of billions in 18 months, then a steep fall as demand shifted from mass primary series to targeted boosters and lower-priced global deals. Pfizer captured the largest share in 2021-22; Moderna rode mRNA momentum but saw sharper revenue drops; AstraZeneca and J&J earned far less and were sidelined by safety/perception and supply choices.

instagram_caption:
🚨 From $0 to tens of billions — then back toward $0.

This is the story of the COVID vaccine jackpot: how four companies turned a late-2020 emergency approval into a once-in-a-century revenue spike — and what happened when the world stopped buying at the same fever pitch.

In the visual you’re about to watch, every year from 2005–2019 is flatline: $0 for COVID vaccine sales. Then 2020 registers the first small advance purchases (Pfizer = $0.5B; AstraZeneca $0.1B). 2021 exploded: Pfizer booked $36.8B from Comirnaty; Moderna took in $18.4B for Spikevax. AstraZeneca and J&J, while critical to global rollout, earned far smaller sums — about $3.7B and $0.5B respectively in 2021.

2022 was the hangover. Pfizer’s Comirnaty still pulled in roughly $32.0B but dropped from peak pricing and one-off large government bulk buys. Moderna plunged to about $8.0B. By 2023 and into 2024 revenue normalized toward targeted booster campaigns and lower-price global procurement: Pfizer fell to roughly $14.6B (2023) and an estimated $7.2B in 2024; Moderna to $3.4B (2023) and $1.2B (2024); AstraZeneca and J&J trended toward negligible COVID vaccine revenue.

Why the crash? A mix of maturing immunity, cheaper competitors, changing procurement strategies, indemnity negotiations, and the pivot from universal primary series buys to seasonal or high-risk-targeted boosters. The video shows the dramatic contrast: Pfizer’s peak vs. J&J’s relative collapse — a real money story built on science, contracts and geopolitics.

Which twist surprised you most — Pfizer’s dominance, Moderna’s rollercoaster, or AstraZeneca/J&J being sidelined? Tell me in the comments.
